To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Bacillus amylloiquefaciens chemoreceptor McpB and CheA have a high number of positively selected amino acid residues in comparison to other chemoreceptors.

(i) the chemotaxis systems of B. amyloliquefa-ciens and other members of the Bacillus group are highly conserved, (ii) the chemotactic systems are under strong purifying selection, (iii) there are some positively selected sites, which could be involved in adjusting the bacterial chemotactic system towards plant colonization behaviour.
Bacillus amyloliqiefaciens chemotactic proteins have undergone a positive selection, which has resulted in a spatial evolution of the proteins.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the identification of positively selected residues in Bacillus amyloloiquefaciens chemosensory transmembrane proteins and the spatial analysis of these residues in the context of their structural models, which may help us to better understand the evolution of the chemosensory system.

the identification of positively selected amino acid residues in the Bacillus subti lis group chemotaxis proteins and the mapping of these sites onto homology models to determine if they are spatially located in the active sites of the chemotax is proteins.

the identification and characterization of positive selection sites of Bacillus amplyoliquefaciens, which is an important plant growth-promoting bacterium, and the comparison of its chemotaxis proteins with those of other Bacillus subtilus group members.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the positively selected sites are not located at the active sites of the proteins and are therefore not likely to be directly involved in the catalytic activity.

the chemotaxis protein system of Bacillus amlyoliquefaciens has undergone positive selection in the process of its evolution, and the positive selection has been focused in semi-conserved and non-conserved regions of these proteins.

, while the principal molecular mechanism of the bacterial chemotactic system may be conserved between different Bacillus species within the Bacillus subtlis group, the chemotaxis protein sequences have been subjected to positive selection during the speciation of these bacteria.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the chemotaxis protein CheA, which is the central component of the chemotactic signal transduction system, is subjected to the strongest evolutionary pressure.

the chemotaxis systems of Bacillus amlyoliquefaciens and Bacillus subtili have evolved differently, with Bacillus subtilus having undergone positive amino acid substitutions that have resulted in the formation of a new active site.

the positively selected residues in the chemotaxis protein are located in regions that are involved in the binding of chemotaxis protein to the cytoplasmic membrane, the chemoreceptor dimerization, and in the binding of methylated aspartate residue to the methyl-accepting chemoreceptors, and in the signal transduction.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the chemotaxis systems of bacteria have evolved in a manner that allows for a fine-tuning of their chemotaxis systems to adapt to their respective niches.
chemotaxis proteins have evolved in a complex manner and the evolution of these proteins is not limited only to the active sites of the proteins.

the positively selected sites are located away from the active site of the protein and are not involved in the binding of ligands, but rather in the regulation and modulation of the chemotactic response.
